newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Cosmonauts shape up for risky repairs to Mir.
newsitem.headline: Cosmonauts shape up for risky repairs to Mir.

text.p: Mission control on Monday instructed the Russian crew of the crash-damaged Mir space station to undertake a daring spacewalk inside the station to repair its power supply.

Reporters at the control centre near Moscow heard a radio exchange in which the deputy head of the Russian-American mission, Vladimir Solovyov, told the two Russian cosmonauts to choose a module of the Mir where they could train for the repair work in spacesuits.
"You have to concentrate on physical exercise, diet and have to drink at least two litres of water a day," a doctor said during the morning radio contact.

Solovyov said pressure, humidity, and oxygen levels on the station were normal and that Russian experts had prepared all the equipment needed for the repairs to Mir's power supply and would ship it to the Baikonur launch pad later on Monday.
American astronaut Michael Foale told an official from the U.S. space agency NASA at Korolyov that he felt fine. "I think we're in good shape here," he said from Mir.

A mission control spokeswoman said the three men -- two Russian cosmonauts and the British-born Foale -- had spent a peaceful night. "Medical equipment showed no divergence from the norm," she told Reuters.
The crew looked well and confident on Sunday in their first television link with Earth since their accident in orbit last Wednesday. All three were smiling and looked fit.

But Foale said on Monday he still did not have a permanent place to sleep after the accident, in which Mir lost between 30 and 40 percent of its electric power potential after colliding with the cargo craft during a manual docking manoeuvre.

"I'm kind of like the dog that lives on the street," said Foale. "We'll figure out where to put me in the end...I can't stay long in there...it's a bit dark...and cold," he added, referring to power problems affecting some of the modules.

The Spektr scientific module, which was already docked with Mir, was holed during the collision and the two Russians will have to don spacesuits to enter it, while Foale sits in the escape capsule in case they need to make a quick getaway.

The Russians must install a modified hatch in Spektr's doorway so that cables can be connected to tap electricity from its solar arrays. NASA officials have said that if the hatch cannot be resealed, the crew will have to abandon ship.
Solovyov told reporters the Progress cargo craft containing the necessary repair equipment was due to be launched from Baikonur on July 5 and dock with Mir two days later.

He said 20 electric cables, hermetic electric connections and a specially-devised "hermoplate" needed for station power-supply repairs would be flown to Baikonur, in the steppes of Kazakhstan, later on Monday.
Solovyov said the crew would leave the job of sealing the hole in the Spektr science module to a fresh team.
"This crew has not been trained to do this kind of repairs (sealing). The work is really difficult...Hermetic sealing will be done by a new crew, due to replace this one in August."
French astronaut Leopold Eyharts is one member of that new three-man crew, which is due to leave for Mir on August 5.
He told Reuters the mission was on schedule. "Now that the situation has stabilised, there is no reason not to be confident," Eyharts said.

"The current occupants have plenty of work ahead to rehabilitate the basic functions of the station and I don't think the mission controllers would want to increase the pressure they are already under. They will leave that to a "fresher" team," he said, referring to the hermetic sealing.

Eyharts, who would be the fifth French citizen to work on a Russian orbital mission, is undergoing intensive training at Star City near Moscow along with Russian cosmonauts Pavel Vinogradov and Anatoly Solovyov for a planned 21 days on Mir.
